title: Archimedes Pi Bounds: 223/71 < π < 22/7
description: Archimedes' classical bounds on π from inscribed and circumscribed 96-gons: 223/71 < π < 22/7. Framework proved, tight π bounds pending.

meta.author: Archimedes (c. 250 BCE), formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib
originalContributions: Archimedes' lower bound: 223/71 < π (2 sorries — needs tight π bound)
Archimedes' upper bound: π < 22/7 (2 sorries — needs tight π bound)
Error estimates: π within 1/497 of both bounds
General inscribed polygon bound: n·sin(π/n) < π for all n ≥ 1 (sorry-free)

overview.historicalContext: Archimedes computed the first rigorous bounds on π around 250 BCE by inscribing and circumscribing regular 96-gons around a circle. Starting from a hexagon and repeatedly doubling sides (6→12→24→48→96), he obtained 223/71 < π < 22/7.
overview.problemStatement: Prove Archimedes' bounds: 223/71 < π < 22/7, equivalently 3 + 10/71 < π < 3 + 1/7.
overview.proofStrategy: The tight π bounds require precision beyond Mathlib's standard pi_gt_d2 (π > 3.14). The framework (gap computation, error estimates, general polygon bound) is fully proved. The 2 sorry targets are candidates for Aristotle proof search or interval arithmetic.
keyInsights: The gap 22/7 − 223/71 = 1/497 ≈ 0.002 — Archimedes' bounds are remarkably tight for 250 BCE.
The general inscribed polygon bound n·sin(π/n) < π follows directly from sin(x) < x for x > 0.
Mathlib provides π > 3.14 and π < 3.15 but these are insufficient for Archimedes' specific bounds.

sections.title: Archimedes' Bounds
sections.summary: Lower bound 223/71 < π and upper bound π < 22/7. Currently sorry — require tighter π bounds than Mathlib's standard 2-decimal approximation.

sections.title: Derived Results
sections.summary: Traditional formulations, gap computation (exact: 1/497), error estimates, and the 22/7 overestimate bound.

sections.title: General Polygon Bound
sections.summary: The general inscribed polygon half-perimeter n·sin(π/n) < π for n ≥ 1, proved sorry-free from sin(x) < x.

conclusion.summary: Framework for Archimedes' bounds is complete with 2 sorry targets for the tight π approximations. All other results (8 theorems) are fully proved.
conclusion.implications: Formalizes the classical method of exhaustion for computing pi bounds, bridging ancient geometry with modern proof assistants.
openQuestions: Can Mathlib's interval arithmetic or norm_num extensions provide the tight π bounds?
Can the half-angle doubling method (Archimedes' actual approach) be formalized to prove the bounds constructively?
